summary: Defines a general-purpose Document-Signing KeyPurposeId for the Extended Key Usage extension of X.509 certificates, building on the key purposes in RFC 5280. Document-signing applications can require the extension to mark certificates meant for signing documents. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A certificate can carry a label saying what it may be used for. This adds a label for signing documents, so a signing app can pick the right ID.

subtitle: A dedicated label that says a certificate's key is meant for signing documents people will read.

tldr.problem: There is no public, general KeyPurposeId for Document Signing, so people reuse email protection, code signing or vendor-defined identifiers, which can cause unexpected side effects across ecosystems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the KeyPurposeId id-kp-documentSigning for the Extended Key Usage extension of X.509 certificates. Applications that verify document signatures MAY require it.
tldr.outcome: Certificates for document signing can be told apart from S/MIME, code signing and TLS client certificates. It is a Proposed Standard and the RFC says it adds no new security or privacy concerns.

today: RFC 9336 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2022, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Document Signing Needs Its Own Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 5280 defines several extended key purpose identifiers, called KeyPurposeIds, for X.509 certificates. The IANA registry of PKIX extended key purposes holds more. Yet there is no public, general identifier explicitly assigned for Document Signing.

The current practice is to use id-kp-emailProtection, id-kp-codeSigning or a vendor-defined KeyPurposeId. The RFC calls using anyExtendedKeyUsage bad practice for publicly trusted certificates.

Borrowing the email or code signing purposes is risky. Technical or policy changes in the code signing and S/MIME world may cause unexpected behaviors, or reduce cryptographic agility, for document signing, and the reverse. Vendor-defined identifiers are fine inside a PKI the vendor governs, but it is not favorable to use one for documents the vendor does not govern.
sections.eli5: People were borrowing the badge line for email or for software to sign documents. When the rules for those changed, document signing got broken by accident. A separate line avoids that.

sections.title: The id-kp-documentSigning Identifier
sections.content:
The RFC defines one new KeyPurposeId, id-kp-documentSigning. Putting it in a certificate's Extended Key Usage (EKU) extension indicates that the public key has been certified for cryptographic operations on contents that are consumed by people.

"Document Signing" here means digitally signing content meant to be shown to a person in a printable or displayable form, rather than processed by machines.

The identifier is assigned under the PKIX key purpose arc as { id-kp 36 }. As RFC 5280 says, if the EKU extension is present the certificate MUST only be used for one of the purposes indicated, and when several are listed an application need not recognize all of them as long as the intended one is present. The extension may be critical or non-critical, at the issuer's option.

Document-Signing applications MAY require that the EKU extension be present and that id-kp-documentSigning be indicated for a certificate to be acceptable.
sections.eli5: The new badge line has its own number, 36. A signing app can say: I only accept badges that have this line.

sections.title: How a Relying Party Checks It
sections.content:
The intended use case is people reading signed documents. The signature tells the recipient that the content has not changed since it was signed by the identity named as the certificate's subject. To validate such a signature, implementations MAY follow a procedure that looks at the KeyPurposeIds in the EKU extension.

  • If no restrictions are set for the relying party and its software, the certificate is acceptable.
  • If restrictions are set, the KeyPurposeIds are processed against Excluded and Permitted lists. Excluded restrictions are processed first, then Permitted ones.

An Excluded KeyPurposeId is one the relying party prohibits, for example the presence of anyExtendedKeyUsage or the complete absence of the EKU extension. A certificate that matches is rejected. A Permitted KeyPurposeId is one the relying party accepts, for example id-kp-documentSigning or protocol-specific purposes relevant to Document Signing. A certificate that matches none is rejected.

Software that handles several data formats may make the excluded and permitted decisions separately per format, for example TEXT and PDF. Restricting combinations of KeyPurposeIds is possible but outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: A checker first throws out badges with a banned line, then looks for at least one line it likes. No fitting line means no entry.

sections.title: What Certification Authorities Do
sections.content:
A certification authority's procedures and practices MUST ensure that the correct EKU values are inserted in each certificate it issues.

Unless the certificates are governed by a vendor-specific PKI, certificates that indicate usage for Document Signing MAY include id-kp-documentSigning. Including it does not preclude including other KeyPurposeIds.
sections.eli5: The people who print the badges must put the right lines on each one. They may add the document signing line, and other lines can stay too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The new purpose is an alternative to using id-kp-emailProtection for non-email purposes and id-kp-codeSigning for signing objects other than binary code. According to the RFC it introduces no new security risks. It reduces existing ones by separating document signing from purposes used by communication protocols such as TLS (id-kp-clientAuth) and S/MIME (id-kp-emailProtection), which minimizes the risk of cross-protocol attacks.

A relying party may additionally prohibit specific combinations of KeyPurposeIds. The RFC also notes the identifier can serve as a stop-gap for protocols that intend to define their own Document-Signing KeyPurposeId, or that lack the resources to manage one.
sections.eli5: Keeping signing badges separate from login and email badges means a trick that works with one kind cannot easily be used with another.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered decimal value 36 with the description id-kp-documentSigning in the "SMI Security for PKIX Extended Key Purpose" registry (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3).

It also registered decimal value 104, id-mod-docsign-eku, in the "SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier" registry (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.0) for the ASN.1 module in Appendix A, which holds the complete definition of the identifier.
sections.eli5: The official list of badge lines got two new entries: one for the signing line and one for the file that describes it.
